summary: A Budget Bytes how-to by Beth explaining how to make soft boiled eggs with firm whites and a liquid yolk using a steaming method with only one inch of water. The core recipe is six minutes of steaming for a large cold egg, followed by an ice bath and peeling, with timing guidance for other doneness levels and tips on reheating and serving.
one_line: Beth of Budget Bytes explains a fast steam-method recipe for soft boiled eggs with firm whites and liquid yolks, cooked six minutes.
key_facts: The recipe uses one inch of water in a sauce pot, covered, brought to a boil over high heat, to steam the eggs.
The recipe calls for exactly six minutes of steaming for one large chilled egg to achieve a fully set white and liquid yolk.
Steaming for 3-5 minutes produces a liquid yolk with soft, not fully set whites.
The note lists 7 minutes as a jammy yolk with outer edges set and 10 minutes as a mostly set yolk.
Using the steaming method, 12 minutes is described as perfect for a hard boiled egg with a fully set yolk.
The recipe is formulated for large eggs weighing approximately 56-62 grams in the U.S. and straight from the refrigerator.
Other factors affecting cooking time include high elevation, type of cookware, adding the egg to cold versus hot water, and the egg's starting temperature.
After steaming, eggs should be moved to an ice bath, because leaving them at room temperature lets residual heat keep solidifying the yolk.
Soft boiled eggs in the shell last about two days in the refrigerator.
To reheat refrigerated soft boiled eggs, steam them for 3 minutes instead of six in about one inch of boiling water.
The article was published Feb 9, 2014 and updated Jul 13, 2023, with a 4.53 rating from 261 votes.
Beth describes the yolk as a cross between butter and melted cheese, and says soft-boiled eggs are not just for breakfast.
